explanations.answer: It might go back to the house of David
explanations.explanation: That's the worry. Jeroboam says in his heart, "Now the kingdom might revert to the house of David." (1 Kings 12:26) David was Israel's great king, and Rehoboam, Solomon's son, is from his house. Notice he keeps this one to himself, so nobody in the room knows the stress he's carrying.

explanations.answer: It might be taken over by Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in his worry, friend. His fear is closer to home: "Now the kingdom might revert to the house of David." (1 Kings 12:26) Egypt does show up a little later, but only in what he says about the calves. Easy mix-up, and nobody needs to feel bad about it.

explanations.answer: It might be split among his sons
explanations.explanation: No sons in this worry at all. Jeroboam says in his heart, "Now the kingdom might revert to the house of David." (1 Kings 12:26) His fear is about the people going back to Rehoboam, not about who gets what later. The passage never mentions his sons here.

Hearts is it. Jeroboam says the people's "hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah…" (1 Kings 12:27) He's not worried about their feet, he's worried about where their hearts end up. I think a man who is scared about that has a lot going on inside.

Armies sound like a king's kind of worry, but that's not the word here. Jeroboam says the people's "hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah…" (1 Kings 12:27) It's about where their loyalty goes, not who is marching. Hearts is the one.

Riches would make sense on a bills-are-due kind of day, friend, but Jeroboam doesn't say it. He says the people's "hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah…" (1 Kings 12:27) His fear is about who they follow, not what's in the treasury.

True. Jeroboam says, "then they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah." (1 Kings 12:27) That is a big thing to be afraid of. Nobody in the passage says it's going to happen, though. It's the picture he paints in his own heart.

Actually, it's true. Jeroboam says out loud in his heart, "then they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah." (1 Kings 12:27) The text says he thinks they might. It doesn't say anyone plans to, so this is a fear and not a fact.

Two golden calves, friend. "After seeking advice, the king made two golden calves…" (1 Kings 12:28) The text says he sought advice first, but it doesn't tell us from whom. I'd have wanted a second opinion on that one, and maybe a third.

Bronze pillars are in the Bible, but not here. Hiram of Tyre, a bronze worker, cast two pillars for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:13-15, 21). What Jeroboam makes is different: "two golden calves." (1 Kings 12:28)

Golden cherubim did exist, and they sat in Solomon's temple, in the inner sanctuary (1 Kings 6:23, 28). That's not what Jeroboam makes, though. The text says the king "made two golden calves." (1 Kings 12:28) Close on the gold, but a very different shape.

explanations.answer: The gods who brought them out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's what he tells them: "Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 12:28) Hold on, because that is a big claim to hang on a calf. The text records what he says, and I'll let that line sit there.

explanations.answer: Signs that the LORD chose Jeroboam
explanations.explanation: Nothing here about the LORD choosing him. Jeroboam says, "Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 12:28) The calves are presented as the ones who did the bringing out. That's the line to remember.

explanations.answer: Guards to keep the land of Israel safe
explanations.explanation: Guards would be a nice idea for a worried king, but that isn't what he says. He tells the people, "Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 12:28) The calves are called gods, not guards.

Dan it is. "One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan." (1 Kings 12:29) Two calves, two places, and the people walk as far as Dan in verse 30. That's a long walk to take for the wrong reason.

Shiloh is a real place in Israel's story, but it isn't on this list of stops. The text says, "One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan." (1 Kings 12:29) Bethel and Dan are the two spots, friend.
Hebron is another real place, but Jeroboam doesn't put a calf there. "One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan." (1 Kings 12:29) Dan is the answer, and Bethel keeps it company.

explanations.answer: People from every class who aren't Levites
explanations.explanation: Right. Jeroboam "appointed from every class of people priests who were not Levites." (1 Kings 12:31) The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve at God's house. He picks people from all over, which tells you this was a brand new system, one he made up himself.

explanations.answer: Only Levites who came up from Judah
explanations.explanation: It's actually the opposite, friend. Jeroboam appointed "from every class of people priests who were not Levites." (1 Kings 12:31) So the Levites weren't the ones he chose. That's the detail the text wants us to notice.

explanations.answer: Only elders who once served Solomon
explanations.explanation: Elders who served Solomon, David's son and Israel's late king, are not mentioned here at all. The text says Jeroboam "appointed from every class of people priests who were not Levites." (1 Kings 12:31) Every class means anybody, not a short list of old advisors.

True. Jeroboam "ordained a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the feast that was in Judah…" (1 Kings 12:32) So he's copying the look of something that already exists. A copy can look a lot like the original, but the text keeps showing us what's different about it.

It's actually true. The text says Jeroboam "ordained a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the feast that was in Judah…" (1 Kings 12:32) He builds it to look like the one in Judah. Looking alike is the point, friend.

Jeroboam himself. The text says, "he offered sacrifices on the altar; he made this offering in Bethel to sacrifice to the calves he had set up…" (1 Kings 12:32) The king is up front doing it. He also installs priests in Bethel, but he's the one named at the altar.

No Levites from Judah in this scene. The text says Jeroboam "offered sacrifices on the altar," and that was at Bethel, in front of the calves he'd set up. (1 Kings 12:32) He's the one at the altar. I'd say the Levites were not on his guest list.

The elders of Israel don't show up at this altar. The text says Jeroboam "offered sacrifices on the altar; he made this offering in Bethel to sacrifice to the calves he had set up…" (1 Kings 12:32) The king himself is the one named, friend.

Not quite. The text calls it "a month of his own choosing," and that means Jeroboam picked it. (1 Kings 12:33) He didn't get it from God. When a feast is on a day somebody made up, you've got to ask who the party is really for.
False is right, friend. The text says it was "a month of his own choosing," so Jeroboam picked it himself. (1 Kings 12:33) The date wasn't handed to him. He chose the eighth month on his own.
